nameStory: This cheerful little plant gets its 'woodsorrel' name from its sour-tasting leaves that contain oxalic acid - the same compound that makes rhubarb tangy. The 'upright' part of its name distinguishes it from its creeping cousins, as this species stands tall rather than sprawling along the ground.
description: Upright yellow woodsorrel is a small herbaceous plant that grows 6-18 inches tall with a distinctly upright posture. Its most recognizable feature is the bright yellow, five-petaled flowers that bloom above heart-shaped leaflets arranged in groups of three, resembling a clover. The entire plant has a delicate, soft appearance but grows in dense colonies that can carpet disturbed areas. Despite its dainty looks, this is actually a tough little survivor that thrives in gardens, lawns, and waste places.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three heart-shaped leaflets that fold downward at night or when touched, creating a distinctive drooping appearance. The leaflets feel soft and tender, with a smooth texture and bright green color.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright butter-yellow flowers with five delicate petals, about 1/2 inch across, carried on slender stalks above the leaves. Each flower has a simple, open-faced appearance that closes up in cloudy weather.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows in an upright, branching pattern rather than creeping along the ground. Forms dense patches through underground runners, creating colonies of erect stems.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces distinctive pointed seed pods that look like tiny green bananas. When ripe, these pods split open explosively when touched, shooting seeds several feet away with an audible 'pop'.

idTips.label: Taste
idTips.description: Leaves have a distinctly sour, lemony taste when chewed - pleasantly tart but don't eat large quantities. This sour flavor is a reliable identification feature.

habitat: Thrives in disturbed soils, garden beds, lawns, sidewalk cracks, and waste areas throughout New England. Prefers sunny to partially shaded locations with moist, fertile soil but adapts to poor conditions. Often found as a common garden 'weed' alongside dandelions and plantains.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges early with fresh green three-part leaves. First flowers appear in late spring and the sour leaves are at their most tender.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with bright yellow flowers opening on sunny days and closing at night or in cloudy weather. Seed pods develop and begin their explosive dispersal.
seasonality.fall: Continues flowering until frost, often becoming more noticeable as other plants die back. Leaves may develop reddish tints in cooler weather.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to underground parts in cold areas, leaving no visible trace above ground until spring growth resumes.

funFact: The seed pods are nature's tiny cannons - when ripe, they explode at the slightest touch, launching seeds up to 10 feet away! Kids love to pop them, and this explosive dispersal method is so effective that the plant can spread rapidly across a garden in just one season.
confusionNotes: Often confused with clover due to the three-leaflet arrangement, but woodsorrel has heart-shaped leaflets while clover has oval leaflets. Remember: hearts for woodsorrel, ovals for clover. The sour taste and yellow flowers (versus clover's white or purple) are dead giveaways.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'weed' by many gardeners, this plant is actually edible and has been used historically as a source of vitamin C. However, it's sometimes confused with shamrocks - while it can substitute for the traditional St. Patrick's Day plant, true shamrocks are usually a different species entirely.
compareHints: Among New England's woodsorrels, upright yellow woodsorrel stands tall while creeping woodsorrel sprawls flat along the ground. Mountain woodsorrel has white flowers instead of yellow and grows in deeper woods. The other yellow woodsorrels in our area are very similar, but upright yellow woodsorrel is the most common and has the most erect growth habit.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Mountain woodsorrel differs from its yellow-flowered relatives in the genus by having white petals with pink veins instead of bright yellow ones.
Slender yellow woodsorrel is smaller and more delicate than upright yellow woodsorrel, with thinner stems that tend to sprawl rather than stand erect.
Creeping woodsorrel differs from its upright cousin (Oxalis stricta) mainly in its prostrate, mat-forming growth habit versus the upright's tall, erect stems.
Violet wood-sorrel is easily distinguished from its New England relatives by its purple flowers - all other common wood-sorrels in the region have yellow flowers.
Unlike other woodsorrels in New England which have green leaves and yellow flowers, false shamrock stands out with its deep maroon foliage and white or pink blooms.
Among New England's woodsorrels, this is the only one with large pink flowers - all the others have either small yellow blooms or purple ones.
Great yellow woodsorrel differs from its more common relatives like upright yellow woodsorrel and slender yellow woodsorrel by its significantly larger leaflets and more spreading growth habit.
Pink-sorrel stands out from New England's other woodsorrels primarily by its pink flowers - most relatives have yellow blooms, while violet woodsorrel has purple flowers.
